Volume 14 · Chapter 12

Macro-finance research frontier

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c11

By the endCritically compare frontier contributions and develop a tractable research question.

Capability and research question

Construct a research question that can distinguish two macro-financial mechanisms, solve the smallest model that makes the distinction, and specify evidence capable of rejecting it. Prerequisites are heterogeneous households, monetary equilibrium, consumption pricing, intermediary constraints, and quantitative model evaluation, with identification and inference from Volume 12. We combine these tools; we do not claim an exhaustive survey of every current research program.

A central bank easing is followed by rising consumption, asset prices and bank lending. That observation alone does not tell us whether households substituted consumption across dates, gained labor income, relaxed borrowing constraints, or benefited from dealer balance-sheet relief. Several mechanisms can generate the same aggregate response. The task is to find a contrast they cannot all reproduce, and to distinguish a proved model implication from an identified empirical effect.

Five original cases below provide reusable reasoning tools. Their numbers are synthetic. Local derivatives describe a neighborhood with a fixed regime; clearing results describe a specified static financial network. Neither substitutes for a full nonlinear heterogeneous-agent general equilibrium or a causal historical study. A later research portfolio must document an original contribution and receive human expert evaluation.

1. A dated map, not a ranking of fashionable papers

A useful literature map has rows for the economic question and columns for state variables, equilibrium closure, identifying variation, numerical evidence and unresolved assumptions. “Uses heterogeneity” is not enough: liquid wealth, age, income exposure and access to credit can enter different margins. “Uses a network” could mean payment obligations, funding dependence, production links or statistical correlations. These are different objects.

Mechanisms to compare before expanding a model
ProgramState or frictionDiscriminating observationPrincipal failure risk
Household monetary transmissionLiquid resources, MPCs, earnings exposureConsumption and income responses by predetermined exposureConfounding aggregate income feedback with direct rate substitution
Intermediary pricingCapital, margins, participation and portfolio constraintsCross-asset prices linked to constrained dealers and funding shocksCalling a correlated capital proxy a uniquely identified discount factor
Financial networksDirected obligations or funding dependenceLosses along measured creditor links conditional on common shocksDouble-counting internal claims as destroyed resources
Life-cycle heterogeneityAge, wealth, labor exposure and portfolio compositionJoint age/wealth response distributions and untargeted cohort momentsReplacing within-cohort distributions with their averages

Kaplan, Moll and Violante’s 2018 HANK author abstract emphasizes indirect general-equilibrium transmission relative to intertemporal substitution. This is motivation for testing household income channels, not a theorem that every heterogeneous-agent model has the same decomposition.

A newer example is HANK Comes of Age: Monetary Policy with Heterogeneous Overlapping Generations. The inspected interior labels its version December 2025 and names Bence Bardóczy, Ettore Savoia and Mateo Velásquez-Giraldo. Its introduction compares life-cycle and within-cohort heterogeneity, emphasizing investment-induced labor demand and heterogeneous income exposure. This is the authors’ reported interpretation; the chapter has not replicated their quantitative model. The PDF’s outer FEDS cover retains an earlier two-author, shorter-title citation. A research log should preserve both identities and the version discrepancy rather than silently treating them as interchangeable editions.

Two additional pre-boundary leads were checked on 9 October 2026: Bardóczy, Shanker and Velásquez-Giraldo, June 2026, whose official abstract describes computational gains from deterministic aging and finite horizons; and Brunetti and Frei, May 2026, whose abstract distinguishes bank capacity from nonbank funding reliance and reports use of confidential supervisory data. These are working-paper leads, with abstract-level inspection here. We do not claim to have verified their proofs, magnitudes, code or confidential records. Retrieval after the library’s 6 October 2026 boundary does not turn these selected leads into a complete “latest literature” census.

Each lead should generate a precise next reading action: inspect the household budget and income-incidence calibration; inspect the Jacobian algorithm’s horizon and differentiability assumptions; inspect how funding reliance is measured and separated from common exposures. A statement from an abstract is a reason to read, not sufficient evidence for a technical replication.

2. Heterogeneity changes the relevant average

Let a fixed finite set of household types have masses μi>0 summing to one. Around a stated baseline, let mi be the derivative of current consumption with respect to current disposable income, holding prices and other arguments fixed. Let ei be the derivative of household income with respect to aggregate real income Y, normalized by Σμiei=1. Units are the same real good. The income-induced marginal consumption response is

K = Σ μimiei = Eμ[m] + Covμ(m,e).

The identity follows by adding and subtracting E[m]E[e] and using E[e]=1. It does not require statistical independence, rational expectations or a representative consumer. It does require that these derivatives describe the same perturbation and that the income-incidence normalization is valid. MPCs out of transfers, permanent earnings and asset revaluations need not coincide.

A primitive illustration gives this derivative economic content. A two-date household with income y now, y′ later, gross return R>0 and discount β>0 chooses saving a≥0 to maximize log(y−a)+βlog(y′+Ra), with positive consumption. If the unconstrained optimum is interior, strict concavity and the first-order condition give a=(βRy−y′)/[R(1+β)] and c=(y+y′/R)/(1+β). Thus the current-income MPC is 1/(1+β). If the lower saving bound binds strictly, c=y and its local MPC is one. At the switching boundary the derivative is one-sided. The income response need not equal the interest-rate response because the latter also changes the value of future income and optimal timing.

If household policies and their distribution both change, C=Σμici instead gives dC=Σμidci+Σcidμi, with Σdμi=0. The second term is a composition effect. Follow fixed individuals or use a state-transition distribution consistently; counting movement between bins as both a policy response and a composition response duplicates it. A covariance calculated from different surveys, different horizons or different shocks need not be the K in an equilibrium model.

For a deliberately restricted demand block, write ΔY=d+KΔY. Here d is the initial spending response after all explicitly exogenous changes and fixed taxes have been specified. Supply is locally elastic at fixed prices, the same income-incidence rule recurs, and omitted investment/government/net-export responses are either fixed or already included in d. For |K|<1 the unique solution is ΔY=d/(1−K): subtract KΔY and use 1−K≠0. Iterating from any initial guess converges because successive errors multiply by K. At K=1 there is no solution if d≠0 and infinitely many if d=0. A nonzero algebraic solution for K>1 does not make the iteration stable or validate the maintained economic closure.

Worked case 1: the same average MPC, different transmission

Two equally weighted interior log households have β=(1/4,4), hence MPCs (4/5,1/5). Choose y=10, y′=1, R=1 for both to keep saving strictly positive; these preferences are an illustrative way to generate the local derivatives, not a realistic calibration. Aggregate income increases fall with exposures e=(3/2,1/2). Mean MPC is 1/2, but K is 13/20 because the covariance is 3/20. If d=1/50, the conditional output change is 2/35. The induced component is 13/350, which together with 1/50 gives 2/35.

With equal exposures, the same mean MPC yields K=1/2 and ΔY=1/25. The difference is due to the joint distribution, not an increase in average impatience. A zero-sum contemporaneous transfer giving each high-MPC household t and taxing each low-MPC household t creates direct spending .3t and, in this maintained closure, output 6t/7. The government budget balances because the masses are equal. This derivative is not a welfare result and does not incorporate future tax distortions, altered interest rates or a supply constraint.

3. From a household derivative to a sequence-space system

A sequence-space Jacobian records how an entire dated output sequence responds to a dated input sequence, near a specified path. On a fixed finite horizon 0,…,T, Jc,yts=∂Ct/∂Ys under an explicit information experiment and fixed remaining paths. An anticipated future income change may alter current consumption: s>t entries need not vanish. A surprise introduced only at date s describes a different derivative. Always state whether future changes are announced at date zero, how initial distributions are fixed, and what terminal continuation is imposed.

After composing household, production and policy blocks, consider the exact finite linear system y=d+Ky. If an induced matrix norm satisfies ‖K‖≤ρ<1, the partial sums SN=Σj=0NKj are Cauchy because the tail norm is at most ρN+1/(1−ρ). Their limit S satisfies (I−K)S=S(I−K)=I by telescoping, so y=Sd exists uniquely. This proves the inverse, rather than inferring it from successful code. It also gives ‖S‖≤1/(1−ρ) and a residual certificate

r = ŷ−d−Kŷ,   ‖ŷ−y‖ ≤ ‖r‖/(1−ρ).

Suppose d and K are perturbed to d+δd and K+δK, and ‖K+δK‖≤ρ′<1. Subtraction gives (I−K−δK)(y′−y)=δd+δK y. Hence ‖y′−y‖≤(‖δd‖+‖δK‖‖y‖)/(1−ρ′). Numerical precision cannot protect against a poorly estimated transmission operator. Norm contraction is sufficient, not necessary for invertibility; a noncontractive matrix can still yield a unique linear solution.

For a nonlinear equilibrium F(y,z)=0, continuous differentiability in an open neighborhood of a baseline (y₀,z₀) satisfying F(y₀,z₀)=0, and nonsingular Fy there, allow the local implicit-function result proved in Volume 2. Differentiating the identity gives dy/dz=−Fy−1Fz. This is a local derivative; binding-set changes, discrete defaults, a singular Jacobian or a changed terminal closure require fresh analysis. A household derivative is not yet the equilibrium response because the other blocks feed back. Increasing the computational horizon is a diagnostic, not a proof that the infinite-horizon truncation error is small.

Worked case 2: a two-date feedback operator

Let K=((2/5,0),(1/5,2/5)) and d=(3/100,0). This is a specified linear spending system with two dated goods; the zero upper-right entry is a maintained timing restriction, not a general property of optimizing households. Its infinity norm is 3/5. Solve date zero: y0=.03+.4y0, so y₀=1/20. Date one gives .6y1=.2y0, hence y₁=1/60. The cross-date multiplier from d0 to y1 is 5/9.

An approximate solution with infinity-norm residual at most 3/5000 has coordinate error at most 3/2000. That bound concerns this fixed operator and horizon. For example, a neglected future demand block can change d; the residual test cannot see it. Check horizon closure, information timing, finite differences of the nonlinear model and stability of economically relevant moments before interpreting an impulse response.

4. Financial networks: clearing and resource accounting

Networks are useful when one institution’s payment determines another’s resources. The original Eisenberg–Noe 2001 publisher abstract frames simultaneous clearing with debt priority and limited liability. We derive a narrower proportional-payment system with a strong, explicit outside-creditor condition. No assertion about all networks is imported from the abstract.

There are n institutions with external cash ei≥0 and nominal total obligations bi>0. Let Aij≥0 be the fraction of i’s obligations owed to j, with Aii=0 and row sum at most 1−ε for one common ε>0. The remaining share li=1−ΣjAij goes to outside creditors. All claims have equal seniority and are paid proportionally; no bankruptcy resource cost or asset fire-sale price is present. Payments satisfy

pi = min{bi, ei+ΣjAjipj} ≡ Ti(p).

Both solvency and repayment incentives here are rules of the clearing mechanism, not strategic default choices. A solvent institution pays b and keeps the excess as equity; an insolvent one passes all available cash to creditors. The transpose matters: a row lists a debtor’s creditors, whereas a column collects incoming payments. Zero-obligation nodes can be removed from the liability system and treated separately; this chapter fixes b>0.

Existence, uniqueness and computation. T maps the closed box [0,b] into itself. The scalar min function is one-Lipschitz, so for any p,q,

‖T(p)−T(q)‖₁ ≤ Σi,jAji|pj−qj| ≤ (1−ε)‖p−q‖₁.

Completeness of the box and the proved contraction theorem give one fixed point and convergence from every point in the box. Alternatively, the geometric Cauchy argument from section 3 applies directly. An approximate vector in the box with residual η in L1 has error at most η/ε. Because T is componentwise increasing in p and e, iteration from zero proves p(e′)≥p(e) whenever e′≥e. The same subtraction yields ‖p(e′)−p(e)‖₁≤‖e′−e‖₁/ε. This is a worst-case gross-payment sensitivity bound, not a resource-loss multiplier.

Define equity qi=ei+(Aᵀp)i−pi≥0 and total outside receipts O=Σlipi. Summing the equity identity cancels internal claims:

Σei = Σqi + O.

Thus lower gross payments can cascade without destroying a multiple of the original external cash shock. There can still be redistribution between outside creditors and shareholders. Real bankruptcy costs, fire-sale price effects and lost investment require additional accounts and mechanisms, such as those in chapters 8–9. Summing every balance-sheet mark without consolidating claims overstates aggregate losses.

For a strict default set D, payments of solvent institutions S are fixed at bS, and pD=(I−ADDᵀ)−1(eD+ASDᵀbS). The same norm bound establishes invertibility. The derivative is valid while the inequalities defining D and S remain strict. At a boundary, solve candidate active sets or compute directional changes; blindly extending a derivative across a new default is incorrect. If ε=0, this proof no longer works, though some particular networks can still have unique clearing. A closed two-bank cycle with e=0, b=(10,10), and full reciprocal obligations has every p=(a,a), 0≤a≤10, as a fixed point. Outside leakage is sufficient, not necessary, and dropping it cannot justify unrestricted uniqueness.

Worked case 3: two defaults, one consolidated loss

Let b=(10,10), A=((0,1/2),(1/2,0)). With e=(6,6), p=(10,10), equity is (1,1), and outside creditors receive 10. After external cash changes to e=(1,6), both institutions default. Solve p1=1+p2/2 and p2=6+p1/2: p₁=16/3 and p₂=26/3, both below 10. Equity is zero and outside receipts=7. Gross payments fall by 6; external cash falls by 5. The resource identity shows the same 5 loss as a 3 reduction in outside receipts plus the disappearance of 2 equity, not as a 6 resource loss.

Within this default set, an additional external loss of 1/10 at institution 1 reduces its payment by 2/15 and the other’s by 1/15. Total gross payments fall 1/5, but outside receipts fall exactly 1/10. If external cash of institution 2 instead rises to 7, p=(6,10); institution 2 is exactly at the boundary, so the same derivative cannot be extrapolated upward. A research design needs directed, dated exposures measured before the shock; correlation of bank returns alone does not identify these payment links.

5. Intermediary pricing requires a testable restriction

An interior unconstrained investor satisfies P=E[mX]. A constrained investor may have a nonzero portfolio multiplier; the associated Euler inequality or adjusted first-order condition must be derived from its feasible set. A proposed “intermediary SDF” therefore needs ownership, participation, financing and portfolio assumptions. It cannot simply replace household marginal utility because dealer capital is empirically correlated with returns.

Even if a positive pricing kernel exists, a small traded payoff span rarely identifies its state-by-state values. In a finite S-state economy with positive state probabilities π, let X be the matrix whose columns are traded payoff vectors. Prices impose Xᵀdiag(π)m=P. If v≠0 lies in the null space of Xᵀdiag(π), then m+av prices the same traded claims. For an interior positive m, sufficiently small positive and negative a preserve positivity: choose |a|<minvₛ≠0mₛ/|vₛ|. Thus prices alone do not determine which investor’s marginal value is the structural kernel. This is elementary linear algebra, distinct from the economic question of whose optimization supports it.

If the payoff matrix spans every state, the linear pricing kernel is unique for given probabilities and prices; that still does not identify preferences, beliefs or the mechanism behind the prices. Conversely, a discriminating additional payoff or a justified parametric restriction can reduce the set of kernels. Testing a dealer-capital model should state these restrictions, use held-out payoffs or conditional moments, and address simultaneity: falling asset prices can lower dealer equity as well as be caused by its constraints.

Worked case 4: a zero premium does not reveal constant risk prices

Three states have probabilities 1/3. The safe payoff is (1,1,1), risky X=(0,1,2), and both prices are one. The family m(a)=(1+a,1−2a,1+a) satisfies E[m]=1 and E[mX]=1 for every −1<a<1/2. The interval gives strictly positive kernels. For example a=1/5 gives m=(6/5,3/5,6/5), with variance 2/25. Yet the risky asset has expected gross return one and zero expected excess return. Its payoff happens to have zero covariance with this nonconstant kernel.

Add payoff Z=(1,0,0) at price 2/5. Then (1+a)/3=2/5 identifies a=1/5; the three payoff vectors span all states. This identifies the kernel in the stipulated state probabilities, not an intermediary’s risk aversion or causal capital channel. Calling a proxy “risk-bearing capacity” does not resolve that distinction. The example supplies an exact falsification target: a proposed kernel must price the newly observed Z, not merely fit the old two assets.

6. Ask what additional evidence changes the answer

Let θ describe structural mechanisms and g(θ) the population moments the model predicts. Identification asks whether distinct admissible θ yield the same g; estimation concerns noisy measurements of those moments. The Jacobian Dg diagnoses first-order distinguishability. For g continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of the baseline, full column rank yields local identification when a square subcollection has a nonsingular derivative: apply the inverse-function result to that subcollection. Rank deficiency does not by itself prove nonlinear nonidentification—g(θ)=θ³ at zero is a counterexample. A valid failure claim needs an actual observationally equivalent family or an appropriately qualified first-order statement.

Additional moments must contain new information. Adding a noisy copy of the same aggregate response can improve precision on an identified combination without separating its components. A mechanism test should predict which household group, creditor link, maturity or asset exposure reacts differently after the same shock. Such predictions still need a credible measurement and shock-identification design; model algebra does not establish exogeneity of an observed policy surprise.

Worked case 5: distinguish income and funding channels

Suppose θ=(a,b), with a and b nonnegative channel contributions in response units. Two model moments are g₁=a+b, g₂=2a+2b, with loading matrix ((1,1),(2,2)). Synthetic exact targets (.06,.12) imply the whole line a∈[0,.06], b=.06−a. The Jacobian rows are proportional, but the displayed line—not rank alone—proves nonidentification.

A new cross-group contrast g3=a−b with target .02 gives a=1/25 and b=1/50. The (g1,g3) Jacobian has determinant −2. More generally a=(g1+g3)/2 and b=(g1−g3)/2. Nonnegativity requires g1≥|g3|; violating this with exact population targets rejects this parameter domain.

If unbiased estimates of g1 and g3 have variances 1/2500 and 1/10000 and zero covariance, the linear unconstrained estimates have variance 1/8000 each and covariance 3/40000. These are exact variance identities, not a normal approximation or a confidence claim. With noisy estimates that imply negative components, constrained estimation changes the distribution; do not keep the unconstrained formula silently. The new contrast might be consumption of high-MPC versus low-MPC households, but only if the model and the empirical design really imply g3=a−b.

A research proposal can now be narrow enough to finish: “Does the joint distribution of predetermined MPC and earnings exposure explain an additional cross-group consumption response beyond a model matched only to aggregate consumption?” State the baseline, alternative and discriminating moment before estimating. Include alternative explanations such as differential durable purchases, fiscal transfers, changing sample composition and differential measurement error. Do not retrofit the target moment after seeing which one favors the preferred model.

7. A research protocol that survives a failed result

  1. Freeze the question and version ledger. Record paper title, authors, dated version, persistent identifier, retrieved location, sections actually read, code/data release and license. Keep wrapper/interior conflicts. Classify each statement as a theorem, a conditional simulation, an estimate, a conjecture or an unverified author claim. A citation is not evidence of full reading.
  2. Write the smallest competing models. State household/firm/intermediary problems, timing, ownership, information, government funding and all clearing equations. List which margins differ between models. Solve both under a shared baseline before attributing different outcomes to a mechanism. A more detailed model can fit better merely because it has more adjustable parameters.
  3. Specify the observable contrast. Write the map from theoretical state variables to measured quantities, units and frequency. Verify rank where relevant, then seek global observational equivalences. State instrument exclusion, treatment timing, anticipation and general-equilibrium spillover assumptions. Use the appropriate Volume 12 inference tool, including dependence and generated-regressor uncertainty.
  4. Separate fitting from evaluation. Assign calibration targets, estimation observations, numerical accuracy tests and held-out moments before tuning. Use dated information sets, common shock normalization and identical scoring samples. A residual certificate is not a sampling interval; a good fit is not causal identification. Evaluate a simple benchmark and a deliberately misspecified rival.
  5. Keep a reproducible failure path. Publish permitted synthetic inputs, exact transformation and algorithm settings, environment requirements, seeds if random, solver tolerances and an executable entry point. For restricted data, report access conditions and a schema/synthetic test package; do not claim public replication. Log failures, boundary regimes and rejected parameter draws rather than deleting them.
  6. Decide what the result permits. Report parameter, measurement, model and numerical uncertainty separately. A failed contrast may reject the proposed mechanism, reveal weak measurement, or remain inconclusive; the identification assumptions decide which. Policy welfare requires preference weights, fiscal funding, transition costs and distributional effects beyond a fit statistic.

Proposal deliverable. Write a two-page mechanism memo, a table comparing two competing models, one fully solved pilot, a one-page data/access plan, a predeclared set of fitting and held-out moments, a versioned source ledger, and an oral defense. A ten-point rubric awards two points each for economic distinction, complete model/accounting, identifying contrast, feasible reproducibility and honest rejection/uncertainty criteria. An unclosed budget, invented data access or an asserted causal effect without its required design is a critical failure regardless of total score. An original paper and expert evaluation come later; this chapter assesses readiness to conduct that work.

Exercises

  1. Derive the constrained two-date log saving policy and both local MPC regimes. For case1 primitives y=10,y′=1,R=1, calculate each saving level and verify interiority. Explain why an average-MPC statistic cannot recover K without joint exposure information.
  2. Reverse case1 exposures to (1/2,3/2). Compute K, its covariance term and the output response to d=1/50. For the original exposures, calculate direct and equilibrium spending effects of t=1/10 redistributed as in the case. Distinguish budget balance from welfare.
  3. Prove the finite inverse and residual certificate for ‖K‖≤ρ<1. For case2, add d₁=3/100, compute both responses and the new cross-date total. Explain why triangularity cannot be presumed for anticipated income news.
  4. Suppose a sequence solution has ‖y‖∞=.05, ‖δd‖∞=.001, ‖δK‖∞=.02 and ‖K+δK‖∞≤.62. Derive and calculate the perturbation bound. Is a residual tolerance of 10⁻⁸ sufficient to make this model uncertainty negligible?
  5. Prove existence, uniqueness, monotonicity and the residual bound for the stated outside-leaking clearing network. Explain the required transpose and construct the zero-cash closed-cycle multiplicity example. Does failure of the contraction hypothesis prove multiplicity in every other network?
  6. In case3 replace e with (2,6). Solve clearing, identify defaults, calculate equity and outside payments, and reconcile total external cash. Then solve e=(2,8) and explain why an all-default linear extrapolation is invalid.
  7. Derive the fixed-default-set payment derivative and the consolidated resource identity. At case3’s shocked point, reduce e₁ by1/10 and calculate the gross-payment and outside-payment changes. If bankruptcy destroys 1/5 of incoming resources at each defaulted institution, can the old identity or clearing map be retained?
  8. Verify the full positive-kernel family in case4 and derive its variance as a function of a. If the added payoff Z instead has price 3/10, solve for a and m, check positivity and price both original assets. What does unique state pricing still fail to identify?
  9. Prove observational equivalence in case5 from the parameter line and derive the variance/covariance formulas when Cov(ĝ₁,ĝ₃)=c rather than zero. Explain why rank deficiency at a point is not a universal proof of nonlinear nonidentification.
  10. A referee states: “The newer HANK paper proves that age alone explains all monetary transmission. The 2026 network abstract gives publicly reproducible causal evidence. A proposed dealer-capital kernel that prices the safe asset identifies risk aversion.” Correct all three claims and state exactly what further evidence is needed. Use a six-point rubric, two per claim.
  11. Two models are evaluated on the same four held-out synthetic response observations. A has errors (.04,−.04,.04,−.04), B has (.01,.01,−.01,−.01). Calculate their mean squared errors. Explain why the comparison alone proves neither causal correctness nor a welfare ranking, and give a defensible response if these observations were used repeatedly to tune B.
  12. Produce the research-proposal deliverable in section7 for a contrast between income-exposure transmission and an intermediary-funding channel. Give a tractable pilot, a discriminating observable, one credible threat, an access fallback and a predeclared rejection criterion. Apply the ten-point rubric; several defensible designs are possible.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Household derivative

Differentiate the strictly concave objective: −1/(y−a)+βR/(y′+Ra)=0 yields a*=(βRy−y′)/[R(1+β)]. If a*>0 it is interior and c=(y+y′/R)/(1+β), so dc/dy=1/(1+β). If βRy<y′, the derivative at a=0 is negative, so the constraint binds and c=y; local MPC=1. Equality is the kink. For β=1/4, a=6/5 and c=44/5; for β=4, a=39/5 and c=11/5. Both saving and future consumption are positive. K includes Cov(m,e), which an unweighted or even correctly weighted mean MPC alone omits.

2. Exposure and a funded transfer

Reversed exposures give K=[(.8)(.5)+(.2)(1.5)]/2=7/20, covariance −3/20, and ΔY=(1/50)/(13/20)=2/65. Under original exposures the transfer’s direct spending is .3t=3/100 and output is (3/100)/(7/20)=3/35. Induced spending is 39/700, and 3/100+39/700=3/35. The equal masses make total transfers zero; that says nothing about marginal social utility, behavioral tax distortions or the supply closure. It is not proof of a Pareto improvement.

3. Inverse and dated responses

Submultiplicativity gives ‖Kʲ‖≤ρʲ and a geometric bound on every tail, so S=ΣKʲ exists. Multiplying finite sums by I−K leaves I−Kᴺ⁺¹, whose remainder vanishes; multiplication is continuous, giving the two-sided inverse. If (I−K)y=d and r=(I−K)ŷ−d, then ŷ−y=Sr and the bound follows. With d=(.03,.03), y₀=.05 and .6y₁=.03+.01=.04, so y₁=1/15 and total y₀+y₁=7/60. A date-one anticipated income change can affect date-zero saving through its Euler condition; the upper-right zero was stipulated in this particular reduced system.

4. Operator uncertainty

Subtract the two systems and solve (I−K−δK)(y′−y)=δd+δK y. The inverse norm is at most1/(1−.62). Thus the bound is (.001+.02×.05)/.38=.002/.38=1/190≈.00526316. A tiny residual controls only numerical error at a fixed operator. It cannot remove the separately bounded operator and forcing uncertainty. The bound need not be attained, but neither should it be set to zero merely because the solver converged.

5. A sufficient network theorem

The box[0,b] is complete; nonnegative cash and claims make T map it into itself. Apply the scalar min Lipschitz inequality, sum absolute differences and collect by debtor row to get L1 contraction factor≤1−ε. Contraction proves a unique fixed point and convergence. Iterates from zero are order-preserving under e′≥e, so their limits are ordered. Triangle inequality applied to ‖p−p̂‖≤‖T(p)−T(p̂)‖+‖T(p̂)−p̂‖ gives error≤η/ε. A row of A lists whom i pays; incoming claims therefore use Aᵀ. With full reciprocal shares, zero cash and b=(10,10), min(10,a)=a shows every(a,a) in the interval clears. Absence of the sufficient bound does not imply multiplicity: positive external cash can remove this family, and other network-specific uniqueness conditions may apply.

6. Check the active set

For e=(2,6), solve p₁=2+p₂/2, p₂=6+p₁/2, obtaining p₁=20/3,p₂=28/3, both below10. Equity is zero and outside receipts=(p₁+p₂)/2=8, equal to total external cash. For e=(2,8), candidate p₂=10 gives p₁=7; institution2 has resources8+7/2=23/2 and equity3/2, so it is solvent. Institution1 defaults with zero equity. Outside receipts=(7+10)/2=17/2, and17/2+3/2=10, total cash. The all-default equations would give p₂=12, exceeding its obligation; their solution violates the assumed active set.

7. Claims versus resources

At a strict default set, solvent payments are bS; collect defaulted incoming claims on the left to obtain the stated inverse. Differentiating with fixed b,A,S gives dpD=(I−ADDᵀ)⁻¹deD. Here the inverse is(4/3)[[1,1/2],[1/2,1]], so de=(−.1,0) gives dp=(−2/15,−1/15), gross change−1/5 and outside change−1/10. Summing q=e+Aᵀp−p gives Σq=Σe−Σlᵢpᵢ. If a default destroys incoming resources, payment must use the post-cost resources and consolidated accounting becomes Σe=Σq+O+total destroyed resources. The old costless clearing map and resource identity cannot be reused. The exact new map also requires whether costs apply to external cash, internal receipts or both, and how nondefault treatment is defined.

8. An identified kernel, not identified preferences

E[m]=(3)/3=1 and E[mX]=(1−2a+2+2a)/3=1. Positivity requires1+a>0 and1−2a>0, giving−1<a<1/2. Since the mean is one, variance=[a²+4a²+a²]/3=2a². PriceZ=.3 implies1+a=.9, a=−1/10, m=(.9,1.2,.9), all positive. E[mX]=(1.2+1.8)/3=1 and E[m]=1. The independent payoff Z removes the pricing null direction, but multiple preferences, endowments, beliefs or constraints can support the same kernel. A structural intermediary interpretation needs those additional restrictions and an empirical design.

9. Distinguishability and uncertainty

Every(a,.06−a) with0≤a≤.06 produces(.06,.12), an exact equivalent family. With ĝa=(ĝ₁+ĝ₃)/2 and ĝb=(ĝ₁−ĝ₃)/2, Var(ĝa)=(v₁+v₃+2c)/4, Var(ĝb)=(v₁+v₃−2c)/4, and Cov(ĝa,ĝb)=(v₁−v₃)/4, as the cross terms cancel. Valid covariance requires|c|≤√(v₁v₃). At c=0 the case values follow. The function θ³ has derivative zero at θ=0 but is strictly increasing and globally one-to-one; rank loss need not mean nonlinear equivalence. Full rank is a sufficient local test, not an exhaustive identification theorem.

10. Claims a referee can audit

Award two points for each precise correction. First, the inspected introduction emphasizes life-cycle and within-cohort variation interacting with income and investment; it does not prove universal age-only transmission. Read the model, nested comparisons, moment targets and robustness before making quantitative claims. Second, an abstract reporting confidential supervisory data is neither public reproducibility nor a checked causal design. Inspect identification, access terms, code and permitted synthetic or disclosure-safe tests. Third, the safe price fixes only E[m]; it does not even identify state pricing in general, much less risk aversion. Derive participation and portfolio conditions and test additional independent payoff moments. All three corrections must separate the inspected evidence from work still required.

11. Evaluation without overclaiming

MSE(A)=.04²=1/625=.0016; MSE(B)=.01²=1/10000=.0001. B has lower squared error on these four common observations. Four synthetic errors do not provide a sampling distribution, an instrument exclusion argument or welfare weights and funding. Repeated tuning on this set converts it into validation/training information; report the adaptation, freeze the final specification and evaluate on a genuinely unused feasible sample or predeclared future period. If none exists, state that independent predictive evaluation remains unavailable and do not label the reused set untouched.

12. Illustrative proposal and scoring

A feasible pilot compares case1 income feedback with a funding block that changes firms’ investment while holding household MPCs fixed. Match both models to aggregate output but predeclare a cross-group consumption/earnings response and a firm response by predetermined lender funding exposure. Solve their combined local matrix and check rank; if its columns remain proportional, redesign before estimating. A potential threat is that lenders with weak funding serve firms with unusually cyclical demand. Predetermined exposures alone do not solve selection: specify a plausibly external funding innovation, validate its exclusion, and test pretrends or placebo exposure with the relevant inference method. An alternative justified design can earn full credit.

Use permitted public or licensed household/firm microdata only if access is real. Otherwise produce a synthetic schema and simulation study, explicitly limiting the result to method feasibility rather than an empirical causal finding. Predeclare a rejection rule tied to a confidence set for the discriminating response under stated identification assumptions; also report weak instruments, unresolved rank and overlapping confidence sets as inconclusive outcomes. Allocate two points each to the distinct economic predictions, closed accounts/model, defensible observable contrast, executable access-aware package and honest decision criteria. The supplied illustration earns the design elements only when its missing empirical assumptions and data access are actually resolved; it is not a claim that an original research paper has already been completed.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back. Explain in two minutes why a monetary response, a converged solver and a fitted SDF each leave a different question unresolved. Answer: the response needs a mechanism-identifying contrast; convergence needs a numerical error certificate and an appropriate model; fitted prices need enough payoff restrictions and structural assumptions to identify the economic kernel. None alone supplies causal or welfare conclusions.

Retention check. Without notes, derive K=E[m]+Cov(m,e), state the inverse and network error bounds, and explain why internal payments cancel from aggregate resources. Then name the extra moment that separates a and b in case5. Key: use E[e]=1; bounds are residual/(1−ρ) and residual/ε; each internal payment is one debtor outflow and one creditor inflow; g₃=a−b supplies the missing direction. Revisit this after one week and again after one month using new exposure weights and a different network cash shock.

Next step. Complete the volume’s model project and graduate qualifying assessment as they become available, then move to economic fields and institutions and the later research portfolio. Further specialist study should deepen one tractable question with current primary evidence; no single chapter establishes command of every research frontier.

Sources and further study

  • Kaplan, Moll and Violante, Monetary Policy According to HANK (2018), author abstract — Historical motivation for heterogeneous indirect monetary transmission; original chapter mechanism is distinct.
  • Bardóczy, Savoia and Velásquez-Giraldo, HANK Comes of Age: Monetary Policy with Heterogeneous Overlapping Generations (interior December2025 version) — Dated research lead and version-control case; within-cohort versus life-cycle transmission comparison.
  • Bardóczy, Shanker and Velásquez-Giraldo, Sequence-Space Jacobians of Life-Cycle Models (June2026) — Current pre-boundary computational research lead, abstract level only.
  • Brunetti and Frei, Bank Regulation and the Rise of Nonbank Intermediation (May2026) — Dated network/intermediary research lead and confidential-data reproducibility distinction.
  • Eisenberg and Noe, Systemic Risk in Financial Systems (2001), publisher abstract — Historical simultaneous proportional clearing context; chapter proves its own stronger outside-leakage sufficient theorem.
